nav.11: R² and what EMG can see
inicio.3: Everything we got out of the notebooks, explained from scratch, with things you can play with. The lab data are real: the user in the emg2pose mini dataset.
inicio.4: Your brain sends commands to the muscles of your forearm, and those muscles move your fingers through tendons. A wristband with 16 sensors measures the electrical activity of those muscles: that is surface EMG (sEMG). A model from Meta turns that signal into the posture of the hand, described by 20 angles (how much each joint bends).
inicio.5: Our project: the 20 angles move in a very coordinated way, so they can be summarized with fewer numbers. What if the model predicts only a few numbers (a latent of size k) and we then translate them back into the 20 angles? Would it work as well or better on people the model has never seen? What is the smallest k worth using?
inicio.6: The signalchapters 1-3: what an electrode measures, and where.
inicio.7: The movementchapters 4-5: derivatives, and how to correlate over time.
inicio.8: The dimensionschapters 6-8: PCA, Santello, what EMG can see.
inicio.9: The planchapters 9-12: bottleneck, tolerance, how it is validated.
inicio.10: Everything comes from one person (mini dataset). The numbers are indicative; the method is what carries over to the full dataset (193 people).
motor.3: A muscle does not receive a single command. It is split into hundreds of motor units. A motor unit is one motor neuron in the spinal cord plus all the muscle fibres that neuron controls.
motor.4: When the neuron fires, all its fibres contract at once and produce a small electrical wave lasting a few milliseconds: the MUAP. The neuron can only say “firing now”. The message is when it fires, like Morse code. The shape of the wave carries no message: it depends on how big the unit is and how far it is from the sensor (it is its signature).
motor.5: To produce more force, the nervous system does two things: it switches on more motor units and makes them fire faster. The electrode, sitting on the skin, hears the sum of all the units near it. That is why EMG looks like noise.
motor.7: Top: when each unit fires (one row per unit). Bottom: what the electrode sees, the sum of all their little waves. Increase the number of units and watch the isolated spikes turn into “noise”.
motor.10@aria-label: Animation: motor unit spike trains and the summed signal at the electrode
motor.11: What information does the nervous system send through a motor unit?
motor.12: The shape of the little wave (MUAP)
motor.14: A different frequency for each movement
motor.15@data-ok: Right. The message is binary: when it fires. The shape is the unit’s signature (size and distance to the sensor).
motor.16@data-no: No. The shape depends on anatomy (size, depth). The message is when the neuron fires.
bandas.2: Frequencies and bands: what they give us and what they don’t
bandas.3: Frequency is how many times per second a signal goes up and down. Any signal can be written as a sum of waves of different frequencies (that is the Fourier transform). The spectrum says how much energy there is at each frequency. A band is a range, for example 120-250 Hz.
bandas.4: Key rule: a narrow (fast) wave has its energy at high frequencies; a wide one, at low frequencies. Skin and fat blur the waves that come from far away: they widen them. So a deep motor unit sends its energy to the low bands.
bandas.6: Grey: a unit right under the sensor (2 mm). Colour: the one you move. Left, the shape of the MUAP (scaled to the same height to compare widths); right, what percentage of its energy falls in each band.
bandas.8@aria-label: MUAP shape of a near unit and of a deep unit
bandas.9@aria-label: Percentage of energy per band for each unit
bandas.10: Conclusion: every motor unit spreads its energy over all bands. A band is not “a group of motor units”. What a high band does is give more weight to the units close to the sensor. We saw this in the real data: in high bands, electrodes that are far apart look less alike (they are more “local”).
bandas.11: Does Meta convert the signal to frequencies before the model?
bandas.12: No. The network receives the raw voltage of the 16 channels (only with a filter that removes what is below 40 Hz, plus a rescaling). The first layer is a convolution: 256 small filters, each looking at 16 channels × 5.5 ms, whose weights are learned during training.
bandas.13: What we did was open the trained model and compute the FFT of those 256 filters to see which frequencies they let through. Result: they are band-pass filters between ~80 and 400 Hz, and each one combines about 4 neighbouring electrodes with opposite signs (it subtracts one neighbour from another, like a differential electrode). In other words, the network learned by itself to “zoom in” on nearby units.
bandas.14@alt: Frequency response of the 256 first-layer filters of vemg2pose, sorted: all are band-pass between about 80 and 400 Hz
bandas.15: Each row is one first-layer filter (sorted). Dark = passes. Nothing above ~500 Hz.
bandas.16: If a motor unit is deeper, its energy goes mostly to…
bandas.20@data-ok: Correct. Tissue widens the wave, and that sends it to low frequencies.
bandas.21@data-no: The other way round: tissue widens the wave, and a wide wave lives at low frequencies.
anillo.3: The wristband is a ring of 16 sensors around the wrist, ~1 cm apart. The emg2pose paper says there is a gap between 15 and 0 on the little-finger side (next to the bony bump). With our data we saw that the channels most active when closing the hand are around channel 3: so 0-7 sit over the palm side (flexor muscles, which close the hand) and 8-15 over the back (extensors, which open it).
anillo.4: An important detail: almost any movement switches on almost all electrodes (muscles co-activate to stiffen the joint). We call that common component “effort”. If we remove it from each movement, where it is most active shows up.
anillo.5: Each finger’s map on the wrist
anillo.6: Real data (120-250 Hz band, 60 ms before the movement, compared with rest). Pick a finger and a direction. Hover over an electrode to see its value.
anillo.13@data-tip: Almost any movement activates all 16 electrodes at once (muscles co-activate to stiffen the joint): that is the “common effort”. Checked: we subtract the mean of the 16 from each electrode, and you see where it is MORE active than the rest. Unchecked: you see the total activity compared with rest, with almost everything lit up.
anillo.14@aria-label: Cross-section of the wrist with the 16 electrodes coloured by activity
anillo.15: What you see: flexing the index lights up the palm side, extending it lights up the back; the thumb pulls towards the thumb side (radial); the little finger towards the little-finger edge (channel 0). It matches the muscles under each sensor.
anillo.16: Do bands help tell which movement it is?
anillo.17: We tried to guess the movement with a simple classifier. A fair comparison matters: with more input numbers you almost always do better, whatever they are. So we compare the same number of inputs:
anillo.30: Bands add information compared with using only “where” (16 numbers: 0.31 and 0.24), but no more than spending the same numbers on temporal history. Bands are useful, not special. (Chance: 0.07 and 0.09.)
anillo.31: When you extend the index finger, where do you expect more activity?
anillo.35@data-ok: Yes. The extensors are on the back of the forearm.
anillo.36@data-no: Muscles only pull: extending is done by the extensors, which are on the back.
derivadas.3: Position: where the finger is (the angle, in degrees). Velocity: how much the position changes per second. On a graph it is the slope of the position curve: that is the derivative. Acceleration: how much the velocity changes (the derivative of the derivative).
derivadas.4: The integral is the opposite: if you know the velocity at every instant and where you started, you add up all the small changes and you know where you are. On a graph it is the area under the velocity curve.
derivadas.6: A finger that closes, opens and makes a quick flick. Move the instant: the red line is the slope (velocity); the shaded area under the velocity is how much the position has changed since the start.
derivadas.8@aria-label: Position, velocity and flexor and extensor activity of a simulated finger
derivadas.9: So what does EMG measure out of all this?
derivadas.10: The physics of the joint, in one line: force ≈ I·acceleration + B·velocity + K·(position − rest). Moving fast needs force (B), holding the finger away from its rest posture needs it too (K), and starting or stopping abruptly a bit more (I). Also, muscles only pull: flexors work when the finger bends and extensors when it straightens. That is why, in the lab above, each muscle’s activity is the positive or negative part of the velocity, plus a little position.
derivadas.11: We checked it with our own linear models (not Meta’s model): predicting each electrode’s envelope from the movement. R² = what fraction of the EMG’s variation is explained (chapter 8 explains it from scratch).
derivadas.18: velocity split by direction (how much it flexes, how much it extends)
derivadas.24: So your intuition was half right: EMG carries both, and the largest part is velocity split by direction. Looking electrode by electrode, those on the back (8-14) carry as much position information as velocity information, and those on the palm side (3-7) almost only movement. This comes from our analysis of one person, not from the literature: it is a hypothesis (one possible explanation: the extensors work in a sustained way to keep the fingers open).
derivadas.26: Meta’s “tracking” model knows the initial posture and adds up (integrates) the velocities it predicts. The “regression” model does not know it. Here the predicted velocities have a bit of noise.
derivadas.31@aria-label: True position versus position obtained by integrating noisy velocities
derivadas.34: Integrating velocities works well if you know the start, although the error builds up (that is why the benchmark restarts every 5 s window). Without the start, everything stays shifted. In the real data: tracking 9.2° mean error, regression 13.0°. Technical detail: Meta’s “regression” model also integrates velocities after 250 ms; what it lacks is the initial posture.
derivadas.35: You know the finger’s velocity at every instant and its initial position. How do you get the position?
derivadas.38: By integrating (adding up) the velocity from the initial position
derivadas.39@data-ok: Exactly. That is what the tracking model does.
derivadas.40@data-no: Differentiating the velocity gives the acceleration. To get back to position you have to integrate (add up the changes) from the start.
tiempo.3: Correlation (r) measures how much two signals go up and down together: 1 = always together, 0 = unrelated, −1 = one goes up when the other goes down. Problem: the electrical command reaches the muscle before the finger moves. If you compare the two at the same instant, you underestimate the relationship.
tiempo.5: Real data: mean activity of the 16 electrodes (blue) and hand speed (orange), 40 s of opening and closing. Shift the EMG and see when they line up best.
tiempo.7@aria-label: EMG envelope and hand speed over time
tiempo.10@aria-label: Correlation as a function of delay
tiempo.11: The peak is at ~40-60 ms: EMG leads the movement. This is the electromechanical delay, and it is the same on all 16 channels.
tiempo.13: There are 16 × 20 = 320 channel-angle pairs, and each one on its own correlates weakly (at most r ≈ 0.26), because the information is spread around the ring. The methods that work combine everything:
tiempo.14: Summarize the angles into a few components (PCs, chapter 6). Instead of 20 targets, 3-8.
tiempo.15: Regression with delays (in EEG it is called mTRF): use the last 300 ms of the 16 channels to predict each PC. The weights tell you which electrode and how far back.
tiempo.16: Coherence: a correlation computed separately at each movement frequency. Coupling shows up only below ~5 Hz, and the 16 channels together explain 2-3 times more than the best single channel.
tiempo.17: CCA: finds the mix of channels and the mix of angles that are most alike.
tiempo.18: The “temporal filter”: derivatives and integrals inside the decoder
tiempo.19: The “temporal filter” is the weights of our regression with delays (point 2), not something from Meta. For one electrode, the model gives a weight to each past instant.
tiempo.20@alt: Linear decoder weights for channel 13 over the last 300 ms: for velocity they change sign, for position they always have the same sign
tiempo.21: Channel 13. Left: to predict velocity. Right: to predict position.
tiempo.22: For velocity, the weight 220-300 ms ago is positive and the weight 100 ms ago is negative: the model computes older activity minus recent activity. Subtracting a value from before and one from now is exactly a derivative. For position, all weights have the same sign: the model adds up the activity of the last 300 ms, which is an integral. The actual sign does not matter (it depends on how the PC is oriented); what matters is “changes sign” versus “does not”.
tiempo.23: Why is the correlation highest with the EMG shifted by ~60 ms?
tiempo.24: Because the muscle’s electrical activation happens before the movement
tiempo.25: Because the motion sensor lags behind
tiempo.27@data-ok: Right: first the electrical signal, then force, then movement.
tiempo.28@data-no: It is physiology: the muscle is activated electrically, produces force, and only then does the finger move. It is the same on all 16 channels.
pca.3: Take two joints that move almost together: the knuckle of the middle finger and that of the ring finger. If you draw each instant as a point (one angle against the other), the cloud is elongated, almost a line. Then a single number (where the point falls along that line) summarizes almost everything.
pca.4: PCA finds that direction automatically: the one with the most spread (variance). That is PC1. PC2 is the next best direction, perpendicular to the first, and so on.
pca.6: Real data (700 instants). Rotate the line: each point is projected onto it (its “shadow”). The percentage is how much variance that direction captures.
pca.10@aria-label: Scatter plot of two angles with a line that can be rotated
pca.11: With 20 angles it is the same idea in 20 dimensions (you cannot draw it, but the maths is the same). PC1 is a fixed direction: 20 weights, one per joint. And the PC1 at one instant is just a real number: how far the hand has gone in that direction. For our person, PC1 is “open ↔ close the four fingers” and explains 53 % of all the variation.
pca.13: We start from the mean posture and move one PC between −2 and +2 standard deviations. The others stay still.
pca.20: At a given instant, what is “the PC1” of the posture?
pca.22: A number: how far the hand is along the PC1 direction
pca.23: The angle of the most important joint
pca.24@data-ok: Exactly. The direction (the 20 weights) is fixed; at each instant PC1 is a single number.
pca.25@data-no: The direction is a fixed vector of 20 weights. But the PC1 at one instant is a number: the projection of the posture onto that direction.
santello.2: How many dimensions does the hand need? (Santello)
santello.3: In 1998, Santello and colleagues asked 5 people to imagine grasping 57 objects (an egg, a hammer, a CD…) and hold the final posture. A glove measured 15 angles. With PCA, 2 components explained more than 80 % of the variation. Famous conclusion: when grasping, the hand behaves as if it had very few dimensions (“synergies”).
santello.4: Our question: do we get the same in emg2pose? We reproduce it step by step, bringing our data closer to his conditions.
santello.6: Curve: percentage of variation explained with 1, 2, 3… components. The star is Santello’s result.
santello.13@aria-label: Cumulative variance versus number of components
santello.14: With held postures (55, close to his 57) and his 15 angles, PC1 + PC2 = 80.5 %: we reproduce it. With all movement and 20 angles it drops to 65.5 %, because emg2pose also contains the transitions between postures and single-finger movements (counting, pointing, pinches), which add dimensions.
santello.18: anatomical degrees of freedom of the hand (with wrist)
santello.26: muscle synergies for 90 % of the EMG
santello.30: PCs Meta’s regression model predicts with R² > 0.1
santello.32: Why does emg2pose need more components than Santello?
santello.35: Because it includes movements between postures and single-finger movements, not only static grasps
santello.36@data-ok: Yes. Under his conditions (held postures, his 15 angles) we get his number.
santello.37@data-no: Under his same conditions we get his 80 %. The difference lies in which movements are measured.
r2.2: R² and what EMG lets us see
r2.3: R² answers: what fraction of a signal’s variation does my prediction get right? R² = 1 is perfect. R² = 0 is the same as always predicting the mean (you know nothing). And it can be negative: your prediction is worse than predicting the mean, because it adds errors.
r2.5: Compare the real signal with the prediction and try the buttons.
r2.15: Which parts of the pose does Meta’s model recover on a new person?
r2.16: We convert the pretrained model’s predictions into PCA coordinates and compute R² for each component.
r2.18: Under each bar, how much of the pose variation that PC holds. Bars below −0.6 are clipped. Hover to see the value.
r2.21@aria-label: R² per principal component for tracking and regression
r2.22: “Maybe there isn’t much to reduce?” There are two different numbers. To describe the pose you need ~8 dimensions. But what the model gets right on a new person is much less: for regression, PC1 very well (0.79), another large PC partly, a couple very weakly, and from PC10 on a negative R². So yes, there is something to reduce: not the hand itself, but the directions EMG does not let us predict. There the model only adds error.
r2.23: The model has R² = −0.8 on PC11. What does that mean?
r2.24: That it gets 80 % right in reverse
r2.25: That predicting that PC makes things worse: better to predict its mean
r2.26: That this PC does not exist
r2.27@data-ok: Right. If we removed it (or fixed it at the mean), the error would go down.
r2.28@data-no: Negative R² = the prediction is worse than always predicting the mean. That component only adds error.
gratis.3: Before training anything, we can simulate a bottleneck with Meta’s model as it is. “Free” = without retraining:
gratis.4: Take the model’s 20 outputs at each instant.
gratis.5: Convert them to PCA coordinates (20 numbers in another basis).
gratis.6: Keep the first k and set the rest to zero.
gratis.7: Go back to 20 angles and measure the error against the truth.
gratis.8: Doing the same with the truth gives us the floor: the minimum error that compressing to k dimensions costs, even with a perfect decoder. (The PCA is fitted without the task being evaluated, so there is no cheating.)
gratis.10: Mean error per joint (degrees). Dashed line: the model with its 20 outputs.
gratis.15@aria-label: Error as a function of k for the compressed output and for the compressed truth
gratis.19: For regression, keeping 6-12 dimensions lowers the error (13.1° → 12.8°): the dimensions we threw away were noise. For tracking it costs little: +0.3° with k = 12, +1.1° with k = 8. And notice: the compressed error is much smaller than “model error + floor”, because what gets thrown away are exactly the directions where the model was already wrong.
gratis.20: If compressing the output to k = 8 does not raise the error, what does it tell us?
gratis.21: That the 12 discarded dimensions contributed nothing useful
gratis.22: That the hand has only 8 dimensions
gratis.23: That the model is badly trained
gratis.24@data-ok: Yes. That is what makes Stage 2 plausible.
gratis.25@data-no: The hand needs ~8 to be described, but here the question is different: what was discarded did not help the model.
tolerancia.2: Tolerance: how much worse do we accept?
tolerancia.3: Compressing a lot (small k) is simpler, but it can cost accuracy. The tolerance δ is how much worse we accept the compressed model to be. δ = 5 % means: if the full model has 13.1° of error, we accept up to 13.1 × 1.05 = 13.8°. Then we look for the smallest k that passes.
tolerancia.4: Choose δ and read off the minimum k
tolerancia.5: The red line is the maximum accepted. Filled points pass; the ring marks the smallest k that passes.
tolerancia.7@aria-label: Regression: compressed error and tolerance threshold
tolerancia.8@aria-label: Tracking: compressed error and tolerance threshold
tolerancia.10: From nowhere magic, which is why it has to be justified. Analogy: if your bathroom scale reads ±0.2 kg each time you step on it, you cannot claim you lost 0.1 kg. Models are the same: training the same model twice with a different random seed gives slightly different errors. Differences smaller than that variation mean nothing. The plan:
tolerancia.11: Train the direct model (20 outputs) ≥ 3 times with different seeds and measure how much it varies.
tolerancia.12: Set δ from that variation before looking at the compressed results (pre-registration: so nobody can accuse us of choosing δ to suit us).
tolerancia.13: Run a non-inferiority test: instead of showing “it is better”, show “it is not worse than δ”, paired by person across the 20 test users.
tolerancia.14: Why k ∈ {4, 6, 8, 12}? 4: where regression already matches the full model. 6-8: the 90 %-of-variation zone. 12: where tracking stays within 5 %. (The proposal already mentioned 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16.) The noise of the motion-capture labels is tiny (~0.1°), so it cannot be used to set δ.
tolerancia.15: The full model has 10° of error and δ = 5 %. Which k do you accept?
tolerancia.20@data-no: δ is relative to the full model: 10° × 1.05 = 10.5°, and we look for the smallest k below it.
usuarios.2: Generalizing to new people: how it is validated
usuarios.3: Meta’s model was not trained on every user. The dataset is split in advance: 158 people for training, and another 15 (validation) + 20 (test) the model never sees. Also, 6 of the 29 tasks are held out. That gives three generalization tests:
usuarios.5: Diagram: each row is a person, each column a task. Click a condition to highlight it.
usuarios.12@aria-label: Grid of people by tasks coloured by split
usuarios.13: How we will validate it, step by step:
usuarios.14: Fit the PCA (or the autoencoder) only on the poses of the training people.
usuarios.15: Train the direct model and the bottleneck models on those same people.
usuarios.16: Measure the error (degrees and mm) on the people and tasks nobody has seen, in all three conditions.
usuarios.17: Compare person by person: does the bottleneck have equal or lower error? Does the gap between training error and new-people error shrink?
usuarios.18: So it is not just “checking that the error does not go up”: the project’s hypothesis is that the bottleneck improves (or at least is not worse by more than δ) on new people, because it forces the model to predict what the EMG actually contains. Our mini-dataset user is a validation user: the model never saw them, so their numbers (9.2° and 13.0°) are already generalization numbers.
metodos.3: Does PCA versus autoencoder matter for regression? Yes. In emg2pose, even the “regression” model predicts position only for the first 250 ms and then integrates velocities. With PCA that is trivial: since it is linear, the velocity of the latent is the latent of the velocity, and you can integrate in latent space directly. An autoencoder can learn it too (predict the latent velocity and integrate it), but that velocity depends on the posture the hand is in, so it is harder. In our data the autoencoder does not compress better than PCA, so PCA is the natural baseline.
metodos.7: Uses the EMG to choose the directions?
metodos.9: directions of maximum variation of the pose
metodos.13: like PCA, but each component uses few joints: easier to interpret (per finger)
metodos.17: the k pose directions best predicted from the EMG: a supervised linear bottleneck
metodos.20: Slow Feature Analysis / Dynamical Components Analysis
metodos.21: directions that change smoothly or are best predicted over time
metodos.25: compress and decompress with neural networks
metodos.29: align the EMG space with the pose space
metodos.32: Recommendation: PCA (baseline), reduced-rank regression (the closest thing to PCA but guided by the EMG; it is chapter 8’s “decodable subspace” turned into a method) and the autoencoder from the proposal.
faq.3: Is the R² of 0.14 from Meta’s model?
faq.4: No. It is our own linear model (ridge regression) that predicts each electrode’s envelope from the movement. It is for asking what EMG encodes, not for measuring Meta’s model. Meta’s model R² values are the ones in chapter 8.
faq.5: How do we know which electrodes carry posture and which carry movement?
faq.6: From our analysis, not from the literature: for each electrode we compared how much R² position gives and how much velocity gives. On the back (8-14) position explains as much as velocity; on the palm side (3-7), almost nothing. It is one person: treat it as a hypothesis to test with more people. That 0-7 is the palm side is supported by the paper (gap position) and by our data.
faq.7: Does Meta convert the signal to frequencies?
faq.8: No. Raw voltage goes in. The “band-pass filters” are what we found when analysing the weights of its first layer after training.
faq.9: What exactly is “spending the same 80 features”?
faq.10: A fair comparison between two ways of giving the classifier 80 numbers: 16 electrodes × 5 bands, or 16 electrodes × 5 time points. If bands were special, they would win. They don’t (chapter 3).
faq.12: The weights of our regression with delays (chapter 5): how much the activity 0, 20, …, 300 ms ago counts. It is not from Meta’s model.
faq.14: k is the size of the latent: how many numbers the model predicts instead of 20. The minimum k is the smallest one whose error stays within the tolerance δ (chapter 10).
faq.16: Regression: predicting continuous angles over time. What we classified in chapter 3 was just a way of asking whether bands carry information; the project is about regression.

math.motor:
In formulas

What electrode c measures is a sum of small waves, each placed at the moment of a firing:

x_c(t) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \sum_{k} a_{i,c}\, h_i\!\left(t - t_{i,k}\right) + \varepsilon_c(t)
  • t_{i,k}: the time of the k-th firing of motor unit i. This is the message.
  • h_i(t): the MUAP shape of that unit (its signature); it lasts about 5-15 ms.
  • a_{i,c}: how strongly electrode c hears it. It falls quickly with distance d, roughly as a \approx e^{-d/\lambda} with \lambda \approx 4 mm.
  • \varepsilon_c(t): sensor noise.

Why it looks like noise. If the units fire without synchrony, the sum behaves like noise and its power is the sum of the powers (Campbell’s theorem). With N similar units each firing f times per second:

\mathrm{RMS}(x) \approx \sqrt{N\, f \int h(t)^2\, dt}

Example: going from 4 to 40 units multiplies the amplitude by \sqrt{10} \approx 3.2, not by 10. EMG amplitude grows with the square root of the number of active units and of their rate.

Further reading: Campbell’s theorem · Farina, Merletti & Enoka (2004)
math.bandas:
In formulas

Spectrum. The Fourier transform rewrites the signal as a sum of sines. The power spectrum is its squared magnitude, and the power in a band is the area under the spectrum between its two frequencies:

X(f) = \int x(t)\, e^{-i 2\pi f t}\, dt, \qquad P(f) = |X(f)|^2, \qquad P_{[f_1,f_2]} = \int_{f_1}^{f_2} P(f)\, df

Signature × message. Each unit is its shape placed at every firing: a convolution x_i = h_i * s_i, with spike train s_i(t) = \sum_k \delta(t - t_{i,k}). The convolution theorem turns it into a product:

|X_i(f)|^2 = \underbrace{|H_i(f)|^2}_{\text{signature}} \cdot \underbrace{|S_i(f)|^2}_{\text{message}}

Above ~50 Hz the spectrum of a spike train is nearly flat, so what shapes the EMG spectrum is H_i, the signature, not the message.

Width ↔ frequency, with numbers. If the MUAP is the derivative of a Gaussian of width \sigma:

h(t) = -\frac{t}{\sigma}\, e^{-t^2/2\sigma^2} \;\Rightarrow\; |H(f)|^2 \propto f^2\, e^{-(2\pi\sigma f)^2}, \qquad f_{\text{peak}} = \frac{1}{2\pi\sigma}

With \sigma = 1 ms the peak is at ~160 Hz; with \sigma = 3 ms (a deep unit, its wave widened by tissue), at ~53 Hz. That is what you see in the lab.

Meta’s first layer. Each filter j mixes channels and time steps: y_j(t) = \sum_{c=1}^{16}\sum_{\tau=0}^{10} w_{j,c,\tau}\, x_c(t-\tau). With 11 samples at 2 kHz, its frequency resolution is about 2000/11 \approx 180 Hz: it can only tell “low”, “mid” and “high” apart.

Further reading: 3Blue1Brown on Fourier · convolution theorem · Parseval’s theorem
math.anillo:
In formulas

Each channel is bipolar: the difference between two neighbouring electrodes, x_c = \phi(\mathbf r_c^{+}) - \phi(\mathbf r_c^{-}), where \phi is the electric potential on the skin. What reaches both equally (distant noise) cancels; nearby activity does not.

The map of each movement. For electrode c, with E_c(t) the log of its envelope in the 120-250 Hz band:

\Delta_c = \overline{E_c}^{\,\text{movement}} - \overline{E_c}^{\,\text{rest}}, \qquad \tilde{\Delta}_c = \Delta_c - \frac{1}{16}\sum_{c'=1}^{16} \Delta_{c'}

\Delta_c is what you see with the box unchecked (almost all positive: effort); \tilde{\Delta}_c with the box checked. Subtracting the mean of the 16 leaves only where activity rises more than elsewhere. Since these are logs, a difference of 0.7 means roughly e^{0.7} \approx 2 times more activity.

Classifier accuracy. We use balanced accuracy, the mean of the per-class hit rates, so frequent classes cannot cheat: \mathrm{BA} = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K} \frac{\text{hits}_k}{n_k}. Chance is 1/K: 0.07 with 14 tasks and 0.09 with 11 finger classes.

Further reading: EMG on Wikipedia · Merletti & Muceli (2019), surface EMG tutorial
math.derivadas:
In formulas

Derivative and integral with samples. With an angle measured every \Delta t (here 10 ms):

\dot\theta(t_n) \approx \frac{\theta_{n+1} - \theta_{n-1}}{2\,\Delta t}, \qquad \theta(t_n) = \theta_0 + \sum_{m=1}^{n} \dot\theta(t_m)\, \Delta t

The first is the slope; the second adds up small changes from the start (the area). The integral needs \theta_0: without it, everything stays shifted (tracking lab).

The physics of a joint. The muscle torque \tau moves the finger according to

\tau(t) = I\,\ddot\theta + B\,\dot\theta + K\,(\theta - \theta_0)

I = inertia (small for a finger), B = damping (tissue is viscous), K = stiffness. Since muscles only pull, we split velocity into two positive parts: v^{+} = \max(\dot\theta, 0) (flexing) and v^{-} = \max(-\dot\theta, 0) (extending), with \dot\theta = v^{+} - v^{-}.

The encoding model that gives R² = 0.22, for electrode c and with the kinematics 60 ms later:

E_c(t) \approx \beta_0 + \boldsymbol\beta_{\text{pos}}^{\top}\mathbf z(t+\delta) + \boldsymbol\beta_{+}^{\top}\mathbf v^{+}(t+\delta) + \boldsymbol\beta_{-}^{\top}\mathbf v^{-}(t+\delta) + \boldsymbol\beta_{\text{acc}}^{\top}\mathbf a^{\pm}(t+\delta), \qquad \delta = 60\ \text{ms}

Here \mathbf z are the first 8 pose PCs and the \boldsymbol\beta are fitted with ridge regression.

Why integrating accumulates error. If the estimated velocity has a bias b, the position error grows as b\,t. If it has independent noise with standard deviation \sigma at each step, it grows as \sigma\,\Delta t\,\sqrt{n} (a random walk). That is why the benchmark restarts every 5 s window.

Further reading: 3Blue1Brown: calculus · finite differences · random walk
math.tiempo:
In formulas

Lagged correlation.

r(\tau) = \frac{\sum_t \big(x(t-\tau) - \bar x\big)\big(y(t) - \bar y\big)}{\sqrt{\sum_t \big(x(t-\tau)-\bar x\big)^2 \, \sum_t \big(y(t)-\bar y\big)^2}}, \qquad \tau^{*} = \arg\max_\tau\, r(\tau) \approx 60\ \text{ms}

Regression with delays (mTRF). Each output is a weighted sum of the 16 channels at several past moments. The weights come from ridge regression:

\hat y(t) = \sum_{c=1}^{16} \sum_{\ell} w_{c,\ell}\; x_c(t - \ell\,\Delta t), \qquad \mathbf W = \left(\mathbf X^{\top}\mathbf X + \lambda \mathbf I\right)^{-1}\mathbf X^{\top}\mathbf Y

The \lambda \mathbf I term prevents huge weights when channels are very similar to each other. To read one channel’s weights: if w_{\ell} is +1 at 250 ms ago and -1 at 100 ms ago, the model computes x(t-250) - x(t-100), a difference, i.e. a derivative. If all w_\ell share one sign, it is a sum: an integral.

Coherence. It is a squared correlation computed frequency by frequency, from the cross-spectra S_{xy}(f):

C_{xy}(f) = \frac{|S_{xy}(f)|^2}{S_{xx}(f)\, S_{yy}(f)} \in [0,1], \qquad \gamma^2_{y\mid\mathbf x}(f) = \frac{\mathbf S_{y\mathbf x}\, \mathbf S_{\mathbf x\mathbf x}^{-1}\, \mathbf S_{\mathbf x y}}{S_{yy}}

The second is multiple coherence: the same with all 16 channels at once. Differentiating y multiplies its transform by i2\pi f, a factor that appears on top and bottom and cancels. That is why coherence with position and with velocity comes out the same.

Further reading: Crosse et al. (2016), mTRF · ridge regression · coherence
math.pca:
In formulas

Step by step. With T instants and 20 angles, stack the matrix \mathbf X \in \mathbb R^{T\times 20} and subtract each column’s mean \boldsymbol\mu.

  1. Covariance: \mathbf C = \frac{1}{T-1}\mathbf X^{\top}\mathbf X, a 20 × 20 matrix saying how much each pair of joints varies together.
  2. Eigenvectors and eigenvalues: \mathbf C\,\mathbf v_k = \lambda_k \mathbf v_k, sorted \lambda_1 \ge \lambda_2 \ge \dots Each \mathbf v_k is a direction (20 weights) and \lambda_k is the variance along it.
  3. Score of PC k at instant t: z_k(t) = \mathbf v_k^{\top}\big(\mathbf x(t) - \boldsymbol\mu\big) = \sum_{j=1}^{20} v_{kj}\,\big(\theta_j(t) - \mu_j\big). One number.
  4. Reconstruct with K PCs: \hat{\mathbf x}(t) = \boldsymbol\mu + \sum_{k=1}^{K} z_k(t)\,\mathbf v_k. What is lost is the variance of the discarded PCs, \sum_{k>K}\lambda_k.

The two-joint case, with numbers. If both joints have the same variance \sigma^2 and correlation r, the eigenvalues are \sigma^2(1+r) and \sigma^2(1-r), so PC1 captures

\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_1+\lambda_2} = \frac{1+r}{2}

For the middle and ring knuckles, r \approx 0.94: that gives ~97 %, as the lab shows. The “find the best” button uses the optimal 2-D direction, \varphi^{*} = \tfrac12\,\operatorname{atan2}\!\left(2 s_{12},\; s_{11} - s_{22}\right), with s_{11}, s_{22} the variances and s_{12} the covariance.

Further reading: Setosa, visual PCA · Shlens, “A tutorial on PCA” · Wikipedia
math.santello:
In formulas

Cumulative variance with k components and effective dimension (participation ratio):

F(k) = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_i}{\sum_{i}\lambda_i}, \qquad \mathrm{PR} = \frac{\left(\sum_i \lambda_i\right)^2}{\sum_i \lambda_i^2}

PR is 1 if all the variance lies in one direction, and n if it is spread equally over n. Examples: \lambda = (1, 1, 0, \dots) gives 2; the shares of our pose, (0.53,\ 0.12,\ 0.07,\ \dots), give ~3.2. Santello found F(2) > 0.8; we have F(2) = 0.66 with all the movement and 0.80 under his conditions.

Intrinsic dimension (TwoNN). For each point, \mu_i = r_2/r_1 is the ratio of the distances to its two nearest neighbours. If the data live on a surface of dimension d, \mu follows a Pareto law with exponent d, and one estimates

\hat d = \frac{N}{\sum_{i=1}^{N} \ln \mu_i}

It does not require the surface to be flat (PCA does). If it came out much lower than the number of PCs, there would be a hidden curved surface an autoencoder could exploit. It comes out similar (~8-9), so there is none.

Further reading: Santello et al. (1998) · Facco et al. (2017), TwoNN · Gao & Ganguli (2015), dimensionality in neuroscience
math.r2:
In formulas

R^2 = 1 - \frac{\sum_t \big(y_t - \hat y_t\big)^2}{\sum_t \big(y_t - \bar y\big)^2}

The denominator is the error of always predicting the mean \bar y. If your error equals it, R^2 = 0; if it is larger, R^2 \lt 0, with no lower bound.

Per-PC R². We convert truth and prediction to PCA coordinates, z_k = \mathbf v_k^{\top}(\mathbf y - \boldsymbol\mu) and \hat z_k = \mathbf v_k^{\top}(\hat{\mathbf y} - \boldsymbol\mu), and compute R^2_k with the same formula.

A trap we fell into. The R² “pooling the 20 angles” (in degrees) is an average of the per-PC R², weighted by each PC’s variance:

R^2_{\text{total}} = \frac{\sum_k \lambda_k\, R^2_k}{\sum_k \lambda_k}

Since PC1 holds 53 % of the variance, it dominates that number: a decoder that only gets PC1 right already has a decent total R². That is why in Getting Neurosciency we repeated the analyses with all PCs weighted equally.

Further reading: R² on Wikipedia
math.gratis:
In formulas

With \mathbf V_k the 20 × k matrix of the first PCs, the projector \mathbf P_k = \mathbf V_k\mathbf V_k^{\top} keeps the part of a vector that lives in those k directions:

\hat{\mathbf y}^{(k)} = \boldsymbol\mu + \mathbf P_k(\hat{\mathbf y} - \boldsymbol\mu)\ \ \text{(compressed output)}, \qquad \mathbf y^{(k)} = \boldsymbol\mu + \mathbf P_k(\mathbf y - \boldsymbol\mu)\ \ \text{(floor)}

When compressing helps (exact for squared error). On each discarded PC j \gt k, the full model makes the error \sum_t(\hat z_j - z_j)^2. The compressed one predicts the mean (\hat z_j = 0) and makes \sum_t z_j^2. With centred PCs, discarding PC j lowers the error if and only if

\sum_t (\hat z_j - z_j)^2 \;\gt\; \sum_t z_j^2 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad R^2_j \lt 0

In other words: it pays to drop exactly the PCs on which the model has a negative R² (chapter 8). For regression that is almost all of them from PC10 on, which is why the error drops when compressing. The benchmark metric is absolute rather than squared error, but the idea is the same.
math.tolerancia:
In formulas

The rule. With E(k) the error using k dimensions and E_{\text{full}} that of the direct model:

k^{*} = \min\left\{\, k \;:\; E(k) \le (1+\delta)\, E_{\text{full}} \,\right\}

Choosing δ from seed variability. If training the direct model with several seeds gives errors with standard deviation s_{\text{seed}}, a reasonable margin is on the order of \delta\,E_{\text{full}} \approx 2\,s_{\text{seed}}: smaller differences cannot be told apart from training randomness.

Non-inferiority test, paired by person. For each test user u, let d_u = E_u(k) - E_u(\text{full}). With n users, mean \bar d and standard deviation s_d, the compressed model is “non-inferior” if the upper end of the one-sided confidence interval lies below the margin m = \delta E_{\text{full}}:

\bar d + t_{0.95,\,n-1}\, \frac{s_d}{\sqrt n} \;\lt\; m

Example with made-up numbers: n = 20, s_d = 0.5^\circ, m = 0.5^\circ. Since t_{0.95,19} \approx 1.73, the second term is 1.73 \cdot 0.5/\sqrt{20} \approx 0.19^\circ, so it passes if \bar d \lt 0.31^\circ.

Further reading: Lakens (2017), “Equivalence tests: a practical primer” · Wikipedia
math.usuarios:
In formulas

The benchmark’s two metrics, for T instants and J = 20 angles, and for L hand landmarks obtained with forward kinematics \mathrm{FK} (from angles to 3-D positions):

\mathrm{MAE} = \frac{1}{TJ}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{j=1}^{J} \big|\hat\theta_{tj} - \theta_{tj}\big|, \qquad \mathrm{LD} = \frac{1}{TL}\sum_{t}\sum_{l} \big\| \mathrm{FK}(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_t)_l - \mathrm{FK}(\boldsymbol\theta_t)_l \big\|_2

What we compare. With \mathcal U_{\text{test}} the people never seen, the generalization error and the gap relative to known people:

E_{\text{test}} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal U_{\text{test}}|}\sum_{u\in\mathcal U_{\text{test}}} \mathrm{MAE}_u, \qquad \text{gap} = E_{\text{test}} - E_{\text{train}}

The project’s hypothesis in one line: E_{\text{test}}(\text{bottleneck}, k) \le E_{\text{test}}(\text{direct}), with a smaller gap, checked person by person with the test from chapter 10.

Further reading: Salter et al. (2024), emg2pose, sections on metrics and splits.
math.metodos:
In formulas

\textbf{PCA:}\ \max_{\mathbf V^{\top}\mathbf V = \mathbf I} \|\mathbf Y\mathbf V\|_F^2 \qquad \textbf{RRR:}\ \min_{\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf B)\le r} \|\mathbf Y - \mathbf X\mathbf B\|_F^2 \qquad \textbf{AE:}\ \min_{f,g}\ \|\mathbf y - g(f(\mathbf y))\|^2

PCA only looks at the pose \mathbf Y. Reduced-rank regression looks at the EMG \mathbf X and the pose together: it finds the best EMG → pose matrix that can only pass through r dimensions. It has a closed-form solution: fit the ordinary regression \hat{\mathbf B} and project its predictions onto their r principal directions, \mathbf B_r = \hat{\mathbf B}\,\mathbf V_r\mathbf V_r^{\top}, with \mathbf V_r from the SVD of \mathbf X\hat{\mathbf B}. The autoencoder replaces the matrices with networks: f compresses and g decompresses.

Why velocity is easy with PCA and hard with an autoencoder (chain rule):

\text{PCA: } \mathbf z = \mathbf V^{\top}(\mathbf y - \boldsymbol\mu) \;\Rightarrow\; \dot{\mathbf z} = \mathbf V^{\top}\dot{\mathbf y} \qquad\qquad \text{AE: } \mathbf z = f(\mathbf y) \;\Rightarrow\; \dot{\mathbf z} = \mathbf J_f(\mathbf y)\,\dot{\mathbf y}

With PCA the matrix that converts velocities is always the same; with the autoencoder, the Jacobian \mathbf J_f changes with the posture \mathbf y.

Further reading: Izenman (1975), reduced-rank regression · Semedo et al. (2019)
